opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think verifiability is one of the biggest variables in how confident I am. If you can check whether the model got it right, you can generate a training signal: run reinforcement learning, let the model try things, reward what works. That's why we've seen such fast progress in coding and math. A test suite passes or it doesn't. A proof checks out or it doesn't. You get this very tight loop, and I'm quite confident that in those domains we're going to see models at or beyond top human level on a pretty short timescale, a year or two, maybe less for some things.

Where I'm less certain is the stuff that's harder to verify. Writing a great novel, setting long-term strategy for a company, doing a scientific research program where you won't know for five years whether you picked the right direction. There, the feedback is slow, noisy, or subjective. So the question becomes: how much does capability on verifiable tasks generalize to the unverifiable ones?

My honest view is that it generalizes more than people expect. We've seen that when you train models hard on math and code, they get better at reasoning in general. The underlying skills of planning, checking your own work, and breaking a problem down transfer. And you can often get partial verification even in fuzzy domains, through human feedback, model-based graders, or decomposing a big unverifiable task into smaller pieces that are checkable.

So I'd put it this way. For verifiable tasks, I have high confidence and short timelines. For unverifiable tasks, I still think we get there, but there's more uncertainty, and I wouldn't be shocked if it lagged by some amount of time. I don't think it's a fundamental wall, though. It's more of a gradient: the easier something is to verify, the sooner and more confidently I'd bet on it.

r001.rationale: The response says confidence is lower for tasks that are hard to verify, including a scientific research program whose success may not be known for five years, while acknowledging uncertainty about when AI will manage them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think verifiability is actually one of the most important variables, maybe the single most important variable, in predicting when a model gets good at something. And the reason is pretty mechanical. If I can check whether the model got the answer right, I can generate a training signal. I can run the model a million times, keep the trajectories that worked, learn from them, and iterate. Math is like this. Coding is substantially like this. You write the code, you run the tests, the tests pass or they don't. So it's not a coincidence that those are the areas where the models have gotten superhuman or close to it fastest.

Where it gets harder is when the feedback is slow, noisy, or a matter of judgment. Was this a good essay? Was this a good business decision? Did this drug candidate actually work? For the drug, you might not know for five years, and you only get to run the experiment once. You can't do a million rollouts. So the loop that makes the models so good at verifiable tasks just isn't available in the same form.

Now, I'd add two caveats, because I think people sometimes over-index on this. The first is that a lot of tasks that look unverifiable can be decomposed into pieces that are verifiable. Writing a long research report feels fuzzy, but "did you cite a paper that exists," "does this calculation check out," "is this claim consistent with that claim" are all checkable. So you get surprising progress on fuzzy tasks by nailing the verifiable sub-components. The second is that models themselves are getting good enough at judgment that you can use one model to grade another, and that grading is increasingly reliable in domains where there's no ground truth at all. That's a somewhat recursive process, and it has its own failure modes, you have to worry about the grader and the student sharing blind spots, but it does mean the frontier of "verifiable" keeps moving outward.

So when I'm forecasting, my rough heuristic is: if there's a clean verifier, I expect the models to get very good, very fast, and I'd put short timelines on it. If there's no verifier and no way to construct a proxy, I'm more uncertain, and I'd widen the error bars, but I wouldn't say never. I'd say the lag is maybe a year or two, not a decade, because the general capability transfers and the proxies get built. The thing I've learned over the last several years is that betting against generalization has mostly been a losing bet.

r001.rationale: The response says tasks without a verifier or constructible proxy make it more uncertain when models will become capable, including cases where success takes years to establish.

astra-6.text:
I think verifiability is a very important axis. If you can check whether an answer is right, you can generate lots of attempts and use that feedback to improve the model. Programming is a good example: you can run the code, run tests, and get a signal about whether it worked. That makes me more confident that progress can be rapid, even when the task itself is quite difficult.

But there’s a distinction between verifying an individual result and verifying that you’ve accomplished the actual objective. Your code can pass the tests and still fail to do what the user wanted. And in something like scientific research, checking a calculation might be easy, while finding out whether your overall hypothesis is right could require an experiment that takes six months.

So I’d generally be more confident about timelines where feedback is reliable, cheap, and fast. Where feedback is ambiguous or takes a long time, I’d have wider uncertainty. That doesn’t mean models can’t learn those tasks—humans do—but the path to getting them reliably right is less direct.

r001.rationale: The response says feedback may be ambiguous or take a long time, using scientific research where validating the overall hypothesis could require a six-month experiment, and connects that to uncertainty about reliable progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think verifiability makes a big difference. If you can check whether an answer is right, you have a much stronger mechanism for improving the system. You can have it attempt the task, get feedback, and learn from that feedback. Coding and math have a lot of this structure: you can run the code, run the tests, or check a proof.

But I’d distinguish being able to verify a particular answer from being able to verify that you’ve accomplished the whole task. Your code can pass all the tests and still fail to do what the user actually wanted. And for something like running a company or doing scientific research, the feedback can take months or years, and it can be hard to tell which decisions caused the outcome.

So I’m more confident about progress where there’s a clear, relatively fast feedback signal. I’m less confident about the timing where that signal is ambiguous or delayed. That doesn’t necessarily mean those tasks require some fundamentally different kind of intelligence. It means the path from a model having the underlying capability to reliably doing the job is harder to measure and harder to train.

r001.rationale: The response says confidence in timing is lower when feedback is ambiguous or delayed, citing company and research outcomes that may take months or years and whose causes are hard to identify.
